For $β ≪ 1$ the Galilean transformation is recovered.
Se dibuja $c t$ en vertical y $x$ en hor: $c t$ is drawn vertically and $x$ horizontally, so that light follows the diagonals at 45°. The world line of the origin of $S′$ is the $c t′$ axis, with slope $1/β$, and the $x′$ axis is tilted by the same angle the other way, $c t = β x$. The coordinates of an event in $S′$ are read by drawing parallels to those axes. Both frames see the same diagram; only the grid changes.
Si un objeto va a $u$ respecto de una na: If an object moves at $u$ relative to a ship moving at $v$, relative to the ground it moves at $w = (u + v)/(1 + u v/c^2)$, never more than $c$. The rapidity $φ = "atanh"(β)$ turns that rule into a sum: $φ_w = φ_u + φ_v$.
La cantidad $s^2 = (c Δt)^2 − Δx^2$ es l: The quantity $s^2 = (c Δt)^2 − Δx^2$ is the same in all frames. If it is positive (time-like), there is a frame where the two events happen at the same place and $Δτ = √(s^2)/c$ is the proper time; the order of the events does not depend on the observer. If it is negative (space-like), there is a frame where they are simultaneous, the order depends on the observer and causality is impossible. If it is zero, light joins them.
